newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Court balances economic and social interests of EU.
newsitem.headline: EU Court balances economic and social interests of EU.

text.p: The European Court of Justice expects to hand down the following rulings before the end of the year.
The court is scheduled to rule on the controversial working hours directive in autumn, although no date has been formally scheduled on the court's calendar yet.

-- Britain is challenging the EU Working Hours Directive which tells employers they cannot force employees to work more than 48 hours per week. Britain claims the directive was incorrectly adopted under majority voting rather than a required unanimous vote. (United Kingdom v Council of the European Union, C-84/94)

-- Within the context of banana quota regimes, the court will decide if and to what extent national courts may suspend Community rules, where enterprises risk suffering irreparable harm, until the European court can review a challenge to those rules. (T-Port v Bundesanstalt fur Landeswirtschaft und Ernahrung, C-68/95)

-- The court ruled earlier this year that member states may face liability from individuals if they do not implement EU legislation. The court ruled if there is a "serious and manifest" breach of a defined right, an individual may seek money damages in a national court.

Failure to implement EU legislation was considered a serious breach. Three of the four cases joined by the the court have already been decided: French beer in Germany (Brasserie du Pecheur, C-C-46/93); Spanish fishermen in British water (Facortame C-48/93) ; procurement procedures for telecommunications companies (British Telecoms C-392/93).
The case yet to be decided is Dillenkoffer -- whether Germany may be liable for damages because it did not enact the EU travel directive protecting tourists from bankrupt tour operators.
Advocate General Giuseppe Tesauro advised their failure to enact the directive was a serious and manifest breach. (Dillenkoffer, C-179/94,C-179/94, C-189/94, C-190/94).

-- In a case referred from the Netherlands, the court is being asked to decide discrepancies in technical definitions, relating to flood relief along canal systems, between EU and national legislation.

Also at issue is whether member state judges may apply national rules to EU directives, which are implemented in the member state but where some inconsistency appears, without first referring the question to the European Court. (Kraaijeveld, C-72/95)

-- German steel maker Neue Maxhutte (NMH) has been under fire from the Commission for monies deemed illegal state aid from the German government in 1995. The court denied in August a request for interim measures to suspend the Commission decision and will rule this term if the Commission properly characterized the money as illegal state aid. (Germany v Commission, C-399/95).

-- Whether importers can bring 'Death' cigarettes manufactured in Luxembourg into Britain, acting as agents for individuals, is before the court in autumn. The British high court declared the import scheme illegal, but importers asked the European court to find Britain's block a violation of free trade rules under the treaty.

The application from the Enlightened Tobacco Comapany (ETC) was supported by retailer Emu Tabac Sarl, of Luxembourg. ETC has argued that it acted as an agent for individuals, using EU personal import provisions.
The Court of First Instance (CFI) is expected to decide teh following:

-- In September, decisions are expected in shipping cases Maritime Belge, Dafra-Lines, Deutsche Afrika-Linien and Nedlloyd Lijnen in September. The Commission decided in 1992 the shippers were violating competition law by setting rates under those established by the Euro-African conference. (T-24/93, T-25/93, T-26/93, T-28/93).

-- The court is scheduled to rule in one of the most widely discussed bail outs in Europe. Bank Societe General has challenged the European Commission's decision to conditionally approve state aid to Credit Lyonnais.
In a related case, Credit Lyonnais seeks to amend the Commission decision which required it to reduce its commercial capacity by 35%, in its operations abroad, by the end of 1998. (T-31/96, T-32/96)

-- Twenty-three carton board manufacturers were fined more than 130 million Ecus by the Commission in 1994 for agreeing prices and sharing markets between 1986 and 1991. They challenged the decision in the Court of First Instance and the court is scheduled to review the fines this term. (Buchmann v Commission T-295/94 et al).
